title: Radical amazement
hook: Abraham Joshua Heschel taught that faith begins in wonder
tomorrow: what's the first thing the Torah ever calls holy?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Henrietta Szold thanked a friend for his kind offer and said Kaddish for her mother herself. I'll say it myself. Today, a new week, and a sunset somebody almost missed.
screen: `I'LL SAY IT MYSELF.` → `A SUNSET, ALMOST MISSED.`

segments.voice: Ever looked up from a screen and found the window already dark? A young man in Berlin did, walking home through the streets from the university, his head packed with philosophy. Abraham Joshua Heschel had come there from Warsaw to study. He was turning over some argument, block after block, when he noticed the light was gone. The sun had set. And he realized he'd forgotten the evening prayer. He stopped on the street. What do you say to God, late, with your head full of other things?
screen: `THE WINDOW'S ALREADY DARK.` → `BERLIN, HEAD FULL OF PHILOSOPHY.` → `THE SUN HAS SET.`

segments.voice: He said the words the prayer book gives for that hour. The evening prayer blesses God, who by His word brings on the evenings. Heschel later told this story himself, and what struck him was how ordinary the line is. It doesn't praise a miracle. It praises nightfall, the thing that happens every single day. That became the center of his teaching: radical amazement. Faith, Heschel taught, doesn't begin with proofs. It begins with wonder at the plain fact that there is anything at all, that the sun goes down, that you are here to see it. Awe comes first, and faith grows from it. He found that wonder already in the Psalms: "When I behold Thy heavens, the work of Thy fingers, The moon and the stars, which Thou hast established; What is man, that Thou art mindful of him?" The something to tell a friend tonight: for Heschel, the opposite of faith isn't doubt. It's taking things for granted. The prayer he'd forgotten turned out to be the lesson he'd been looking for in all those books.
screen: `WHO BRINGS ON THE EVENINGS.` · `NOT A MIRACLE: NIGHTFALL.` · `AWE COMES FIRST.` · `WHEN I BEHOLD THY HEAVENS.` · then, large: `WONDER FIRST.`

segments.voice: Pick up one ordinary thing within reach: a cup, a leaf, your own hand. Look at it as if it had just appeared, its color, its weight, the fact that it exists at all. Stay with one detail until it starts to surprise you.
screen: `ONE ORDINARY THING.` · `AS IF IT JUST APPEARED.`

segments.voice: Radical amazement: Abraham Joshua Heschel's teaching that faith starts in wonder, even at things that happen every day, like nightfall.
Pocket this one: wonder first. In Heschel's telling, taking the world for granted is the real danger to faith.
